title: Microstructure, texture, and mechanical anisotropy of dual-phase steel: Effect of intercritical annealing temperature
abstract: The effect of intercritical annealing temperature on the microstructure, texture, and mechanical anisotropic of dual-phase (DP) steel sheets has been investigated. It was observed that by the increment of intercritical annealing temperature, the fraction of martensite phase increases from 0.224 to 0.233 and finally to 0.315 in the 770-10, 800-10, and 830-10 samples, respectively. Eventually, a chain-like morphology of martensite islands was formed, which was beneficial for improving strength-ductility balance. The ferrite grain sizedid not show an explicit trend as it initially decreased from 10.7 to 7.2 μm and then increased to 8.5 μm by increasing the annealing temperature. Moreover, the martensite distribution was enhanced in both RD-ND and RD-TD planes as the annealing time was prolonged. The texture evolution was characterized by the gradual weakening of γ-fiber and decreasing the overall texture intensity. With regard to the Vickers hardness measurements, it exhibited a constant increase from 219.8 to 238.0 HV by the increment of martensite volume fraction. However, as the martensite carbon content was decreased gradually, the increase in hardness was not very sharp. The tensile curves of all DP samples revealed a low yield ratio and continuous yielding behavior. The typical rise in strength and fall in ductility was not readily observed as the annealing time increased, which was related to the different texture components, martensite morphology, and the distribution of martensite in different planes of DP samples. The isotropic behavior of the 830-10 sample was superior compared to other samples owing to the elimination of γ-fiber, the texture weakening, and the uniform distribution of martensite. The strain-hardening rate curves of DP samples revealed a high initial strain-hardening rate and a three-stage work-hardening behavior.
journal: Journal of Science: Advanced Materials and Devices

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Plain low-carbon steels are recognized by their good formability, proper weldability, and cost-efficiency but low yield strength (YS), poor ultimate tensile strength (UTS), and discontinuous yielding behavior [ 1–3 ]. To increase their strength, different grades of advanced high-strength steels (AHSSs) have been developed in recent decades [ 1 , 4 ]. Dual-phase steels (DPs) are one of the most prominent AHSS grades among the first generation mostly used in the automobile industry [ 5–13 ]. Their application in manufacturing various automobile parts dates back to the mid-70s [ 14 ], considering their improved strength-ductility balance, good weldability, low yield ratio, low fabrication cost, high strain-hardening rate, and continuous yielding behavior [ 15–19 ]. However, there is usually a severe stress and strain partitioning between the two phases due to the difference in their plastic deformability, which encourages the decohesion of ferrite-martensite interfaces and the formation of microvoids [ 20 , 21 ]. Another weakness of DP steels is their relatively poor plastic strain ratio (r-value), exacerbating their deep drawability [ 22 , 23 ]. Compared with other AHSS steels, such as transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) and twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) steels, DP steels have a simpler manufacturing process, exhibit better weldability, and possess higher thermomechanical stability in elevated temperatures [ 22 , 24 , 25 ]. Their microstructure consists of the ferrite matrix, which maintains high ductility, and embedded martensite islands, which impart high strength. The relatively simple fabrication process of DP steels is comprised of heating the worksheet to the intercritical (ferrite plus austenite) region, soaking in the intercritical region for a certain time, and quenching the sheet so that the austenite transforms into martensite at ambient temperature [ 26–30 ].

The DP steel properties are mainly governed by the morphology, distribution, and volume fraction (V m ) of martensite plus the ferrite grain size (d f ) [ 15 , 18 , 25 , 28 , 31–33 ]. In past years, due to the necessity of improving fuel efficiency and passenger safety, there has been a surge in the need to further enhance the aforementioned characteristics in DP steels [ 9 , 14 , 22 , 27 , 29 ]. In fact, by enhancing the strength of DP sheets, thinner gages could be implemented which reduce the overall weight of the panel [ 13 , 34 ]. The increment in the carbon concentration and adding the alloying elements to improve the strength has brought about lower weldability and increased alloying cost [ 35–40 ]. In addition, increasing the carbon concentration will harden the martensite phase, thereby increasing strain gradients and plastic deformation incompatibility between the two phases leading to lower interface cohesion [ 41 ]. One of the most promising methods to enhance the strength-ductility balance and improve the strain-hardening capability is the reduction of d f  [ 24 , 29 , 41–44 ]. Furthermore, decreasing the d f  will mitigate the stress and strain partitioning between ferrite and martensite [ 21 ]. In order to reduce d f , different methods including severe plastic deformation (SPD), thermomechanical processing, thermal cycling, deformation-induced ferrite transformation (DIFT), and ultra-fast heating have been utilized [ 25 , 36 , 37 , 43–46 ]. Each of the mentioned fabrication routes has its limits. For example, SPD techniques such as equal channel angular pressing (ECAP) and accumulative roll bonding (ARB) exhibit great potential in achieving ultra-fine ferrite and martensite grains (UFG) with extremely high UTS but in turn, significantly low total elongation (TEL). Furthermore, besides high manufacturing cost, the shape and size of specimens processed by SPD methods are limited which hampers their industrial application [ 37 , 39 , 44–46 ]. An effective way to reduce the d f  is the adjustment of the initial microstructure by different heat treatment schedules. In this regard, fibrous martensite and DP starting microstructures demonstrated promising results. Austenitizing the initial workpiece and subsequent quenching in water produces a martensitic matrix and by applying a cold deformation cycle, a fine fibrous structure is obtained prior to intercritical annealing which provides abundant nucleation sites for austenite encouraging the grain refinement significantly [ 18 , 19 , 25 , 47 ]. Moreover, producing an initial DP structure with intercritical annealing and applying cold deformation with an eventual intercritical cycle also produces a chain-like morphology, significantly enhancing grain refinement [ 5 , 36 , 39 , 43 , 46 ]. For instance, Karmakar et al. [ 45 ] produced DP samples from three different initial structures, namely ferrite-pearlite, ferrite-blocky martensite, and ferrite-fibrous martensite structures. They reported the most significant grain refinement and the best combination of strength-ductility for the fibrous microstructure. Deng et al. [ 14 ] compared DP samples obtained from 60 % cold rolling of initial martensitic and DP microstructures. They reported that the initial fibrous martensitic matrix produces lower d f  and higher mechanical properties after the final intercritical annealing. Among SPD methods, asymmetric rolling (ASR) has demonstrated promising results in recent works on DP steels showing a great potential to produce UFG microstructure. Additional homogenous shear strain through thickness introduced by the asymmetry of rolls improves martensite distribution all over the sample [ 2 , 3 , 19 , 30 , 40 ]. Moreover, compared with other SPD methods, ASR provides a simple setup and higher industrial-scale applicability [ 48–52 ]. Another recently studied approach for lowering the d f  is short-term partial annealing which activates the static recrystallization mechanisms (SRX) producing fine equiaxed grains and spherical carbides with a homogenous distribution [ 38 , 39 , 53–55 ]. In partial (incomplete or sub-critical) annealing, steel is heated to a lower temperature than full annealing (usually lower than the A C1  critical temperature). This can significantly affect the final distribution and morphology of martensite islands after intercritical annealing. Regarding the examination of the partial-annealing effect, the study of Mazaheri et al. [ 38 ] gives valuable results. The microstructural observations in their work revealed the presence of ferrite aggregates and nanocarbides. Carbide particles were almost rounded with an average diameter of 90 nm and UFG ferrite aggregates revealed an average size of 400 nm. The final DP structure revealed a homogenous network of martensite islands surrounding the ferrite grains. This particular structure is beneficial for improving the elongation in high stresses since the martensite islands prevent strain localization to adjacent ferrite grains. Moreover, martensite islands are able to effectively prevent the migration of RX ferrite grains and by increasing the V m  in higher intercritical temperatures, d f  is reduced. Considering that, the d f  was steadily reduced from 3.83 μm in the sample annealed at 760 °C for 10 min to only 1.67 μm in the sample annealed at 820 °C for the same amount of time indicating the substantial potential of grain refinement by the combination of cold rolling and partial annealing.

All in all, to the best knowledge of the authors, no study has contributed to the understanding of the simultaneous effect of ASR and partial (intermediate) annealing on the microstructure, texture, mechanical properties, and anisotropy of DP steels produced by an alteration in the intercritical annealing temperature. Therefore, a plain low-carbon ferrite-pearlite sheet was selected to examine the effect of the abovementioned parameters. In addition, the data regarding the examination of texture evolution and anisotropic behavior of produced samples, which are extensively discussed in this paper, provides a deeper perception of the related phenomena in the fabrication cycle of DP steels.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs:
A plain ferrite-pearlite low-carbon steel sheet with the chemical composition of Fe-0.07C-0.78Mn-0.15Si was used in this study. The initial ferrite-pearlite microstructure is depicted in  Fig. 1 
                      . The ferrite grains (as displayed by pink arrows) exhibit an equiaxed morphology and pearlite colonies (as marked by green arrows) are present in all planes occupying 7 % of the microstructure. The mean grain size of the ferrite phase is 12.6 μm. Furthermore, some inclusions can be seen throughout the microstructures as indicated by yellow arrows in  Fig. 1 (a).

In order to perform asymmetric cold-rolling, workpieces with the dimensions of 12 mm (l) × 5 mm (w) × 4 mm (t) were cut from the as-received sheet. Thereafter, the asymmetric single-roll drive rolling (SRDR) was performed on workpieces using smooth and dry rolls at ambient temperature in 15 rolling passes with a total thickness reduction of 75 % and a final thickness of 1 mm. The drive roller rotated with a fixed speed of 3 rpm and a roll diameter of 150 mm. Subsequently, all cold-rolled workpieces were partially annealed at 700 °C for 10 min and quenched in water (the 700-10 sample). Ultimately, the partially annealed samples were intercritical annealed at the temperatures of 770 °C, 800 °C, and 830 °C (dual-phase region) for 10 min before final water quenching (770-10, 800-10, and 830-10 samples). The Ac 1  and Ac 3  temperatures were computed to be 720 °C and 862 °C, respectively, using two well-established equations [ 56 ]. The schematic illustration of the fabrication route is presented in  Fig. 2 
                      (a).

The microstructural characterization was carried out using a Dewinter optical microscope (OM) on RD-TD, RD-ND, and TD-ND planes from each annealed and DP workpiece. All metallographic samples were mounted and prepared by grinding until 2000 grit finish followed by polishing with 1 μm alumina suspension and etching in 4 % Nital solution. An SNE-4500 M scanning electron microscope (SEM) was utilized for the detailed observation of DP microstructures in higher magnifications. The elemental compositions of ferrite grains and martensite islands were evaluated by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). The linear intercept method was used to estimate the average grain size of partially annealed specimens. Quantitative analysis was done using ImageJ software on all mentioned planes. To investigate the martensite islands’ distribution in the ferritic matrix, an approach mentioned in the work of Yourdkhani and Hubert [ 57 ] was taken into account. Macrotexture analysis was carried out on the RD-TD plane at the midthickness of the sheets by X-ray diffraction (XRD). The incomplete pole figures were employed to calculate orientation distribution functions via ATEX software [ 58 ].

Vickers hardness test was performed on the RD-TD plane of each sample for a minimum of 9 readings using a Koopa UV1 hardness tester with a load of 5 kg and dwell time of 10 s and the average value of all readings for each sample was reported. Tensile tests were performed using a SANTAM STM-250 machine at room temperature with a constant crosshead velocity of 1 mm min −1  for each sample along RD (0°) diagonal to RD (45°) and perpendicular to RD axis (90°) to evaluate the anisotropy of mechanical properties. The sub-size dog-bone specimens ( Fig. 2 (b)) were prepared using wire-cut electro-discharge machining with the gauge length and gauge width of 12 mm and 3 mm, respectively.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs:
Fig. 3 
                       illustrates the microstructure of the 700-10 sample in different planes. As a result of annealing at 700 °C, the deformed microstructure (after 75 % strain) is replaced by recrystallized ferrite grains and a dispersion of spherical carbides mostly placed on ferrite grain boundaries, and a lower fraction in the interior of coarser ferrite grains. The d f  ranges between 1.7 and 27.7 μm. After 75 % cold deformation, high stored energy and dislocation density are present in the material providing enough driving force for the initiation of recrystallization mechanisms [ 22 , 29 , 35 , 44 , 59 ]. Partial annealing leads to a drastic reduction of dislocation density and gives rise to the fraction of recrystallized grains. The grains with higher dislocation density initiate the recrystallization earlier and enter the growth stage leading to a higher d f  as opposed to grains with lower dislocation density [ 49 ]. According to these results, it can be said that a microstructure consisting of fine and coarse ferrite grains has been formed in the steel microstructure after partial annealing treatment.

Figs. 4–6 
                      
                      
                       reveal the OM images of the 770-10, 800-10, and 830-10 DP samples in all 3 planes, respectively. Also, the SEM images of the 770-10, 800-10, and 830-10 DP samples on the RD-ND section are shown in  Figs. 7–9 
                      
                      
                      , respectively. In addition, the mean grain size of ferrite and fraction of martensite as a function of the intercritical annealing temperature is depicted in  Fig. 10 
                      . The RD-TD plane of the 770-10 DP steel ( Fig. 4 (a)) reveals a non-uniform distribution of the martensite islands along ferrite grain boundaries. In fact, it was stated by several authors that the ferrite grain boundaries and spherical carbides can act as preferential sites for the austenite nucleation due to the enrichment of carbon in these areas [ 7 , 9 , 22 , 28 , 60 ]. With the dissolution of initial pearlite colonies by heating, the carbon atoms segregate to ferrite grain boundaries. The easy diffusion path for carbon atoms would naturally be along ferrite grain boundaries. Therefore, by the continuation of soaking in elevated temperatures, austenite will grow along grain boundaries, and the chain-like morphology will slowly form [ 14 , 21 , 28 ]. This can be more clearly noticed in RD-ND and TD-ND planes ( Fig. 4 (b) and (c)) which reveal a more uniform dispersion of martensite islands along the boundaries of recrystallized ferrite grains. Moreover, some isolated martensite islands can be found in the RD-ND plane ( Fig. 4 (b)) further approving that the spherical carbides in the interior of ferrite grains will be potential sites for austenite formation as reported in previous works [ 20 , 26–28 , 53 , 60 ]. Quantitative analysis revealed that the V m  and d f  were 0.224 and 10.2 μm, respectively ( Fig. 10 ).

Fig. 5  indicates a more uniform distribution of ferrite and martensite in different planes. It is expected that the higher intercritical annealing temperature will result in the increment of V m  which can be readily seen from the optical micrographs. This is also reported in previous studies about DP steels [ 7 , 16 , 25 , 31 , 32 , 61 ]. Nevertheless, the chain-like morphology of martensite cannot be seen ideally as some ferrite grain boundaries are still devoid of any martensite islands. Furthermore, high-temperature annealing will provide enough time for the recrystallized grains to grow and reach a higher d f  which did not happen since during the intercritical annealing the austenite nuclei had prevented the ferrite grain boundaries migration and yielded a lower d f  compared with the 770-10 DP sample [ 7 , 9 , 27 , 42 , 59 , 62 , 63 ]. In this sample, the V m  and d f  were 0.233 and 7.2 μm, respectively ( Fig. 10 ).

The same can be said for the microstructure of the 830-10 DP sample depicted in  Fig. 6 . The increment of annealing temperature significantly increased the V m  and the chain-like morphology was achieved. This essentially needs proper control of intercritical annealing temperature and time to restrict significant growth of the ferrite phase while achieving an acceptable fraction of martensite islands at the same time [ 29 ]. Another change worthy of pointing out is the gradual increase of martensite islands’ size in higher temperatures which clearly happened in the 830-10 sample as reported in previous works [ 24 , 38 , 40 ]. Expectedly, the V m  rose to 0.315 while the d f  also increased to 8.5 μm ( Fig. 10 ) suggesting that the effect of faster growth due to easier diffusion at higher annealing temperature has undermined the grain-boundary pinning by austenite nuclei. It is noteworthy that the utilization of ASR was beneficial for achieving a more uniform distribution of martensite islands through thickness which can be observed in RD-ND and TD-ND planes of DP samples ( Figs. 4–6 ).

In the SEM micrographs of DP samples ( Figs. 7–9 ), the protruded areas with a bright color indicate martensite islands whereas ferrite grains reveal a dark color and are sunken. For the 770-10 DP sample ( Fig. 7 ) fine martensite islands are stretched along ferrite grain boundaries in accordance with the optical images ( Fig. 4 ). Most martensitic regions did not exhibit thick islands and a moderate fraction of ferrite grain boundaries do not contain any martensite phase. The martensite lamellae cannot be distinguished due to the higher C m  (carbon content of martensite) at lower V m  [ 2 ].

The SEM micrographs of the 800-10 DP sample ( Fig. 8 ) reveal an almost complete homogenous distribution of martensite islands along grain boundaries. In fact, the extremely fine martensite layers along grain boundaries can be distinguished in SEM images demonstrating that the 800-10 DP sample also exhibits a chain-like morphology, and ferrite grains without any surrounding martensite islands were hardly found. Also, nearly globular isolated martensite islands in larger ferrite grains can be found in  Fig. 8 (a). Furthermore, the fraction of thin martensite layers is reduced and the martensite phase has steadily got thicker. The EDS spot in  Fig. 8 (d) reveals 3.22 wt% C in a martensitic island which is much higher than the initial carbon concentration of the as-received steel (0.07 wt%). The obvious reason is the lack of required time for carbon atoms to diffuse out of their interstitial positions during quenching with an almost 300  ° C/s cooling rate leading to the formation of the super-saturated martensite phase with a body-centered tetragonal (BCT) crystallographic structure. On top of that, it was claimed that during soaking at the intercritical region, the manganese atoms will gradually segregate to the austenite nuclei. The enriched concentration of manganese in the EDS spot observed in  Fig. 8 (d) can approve previous reports [ 53 , 60 ].

Fig. 9  illustrates the SEM images taken of the 830-10 sample demonstrating an entirely homogenous distribution of martensite islands along grain boundaries leading to a complete chain-like microstructure. All ferrite grains are completely surrounded by adjacent martensite islands which almost entirely grew by some extent into the ferrite grains. Therefore, extremely thin layers of martensite are impossible to be found. Because of the reduction of C m  by increasing the V m , the difference between the protruded and sunken regions is diminished and the martensite lamellae are totally distinguishable, especially in higher magnifications ( Fig. 9 (b) and (c)) [ 40 ].

Fig. 11  quantifies the distribution of martensite islands in the ferritic matrix for each sample on the RD-TD ( Fig. 11 
                      (a)) and the RD-ND ( Fig. 11 (b)) planes. The higher and narrower the peak the more homogenous the distribution will be [ 57 ]. In other words, peaks with higher intensities and lower widths indicate a higher density of martensite islands situated in smaller proximities, thereby achieving a more uniform dispersion of them. With regard to the RD-TD plane, the 770-10 and 800-10 samples, both reveal nearly identical distribution being inferior to the 830-10 sample. However, in the RD-ND section, the 800-10 sample shows a more homogeneous distribution of martensite islands than the 770-10 sample relating to the gradual formation of chain-like morphology. In any case, the 830-10 sample with fully chain-like morphology exhibits a more uniform distribution in both planes. It can be concluded that, by increasing the temperature of the intercritical annealing treatment, the martensite distribution in the ferrite matrix becomes more uniform. This result can be related to the increase in the martensite fraction in the ferrite matrix with increasing intercritical annealing temperature. As the martensite fraction increases, the martensite-free areas in the microstructure decrease, which can lead to a more uniform distribution of martensite in the ferrite matrix.

The orientation distribution functions of the DP samples processed by changing the intercritical annealing temperature are depicted in  Fig. 12 
                      . The typical BCC rolling texture of low-carbon steel is characterized by the presence of strong α-fiber (<110>//RD) and γ-fiber (<111>//ND) [ 33 , 48 , 51 , 64 , 65 ]. Naturally, by applying a high-temperature intercritical annealing cycle, it is expected that the rolling fibers will be weakened and other orientations will be developed as a result of recrystallization mechanisms and partial austenitization [ 23 ]. In some previous studies [ 22 , 54 , 62 , 64 ], which examined the texture of DP samples that had undergone a rolling process, the presence of a relatively weak α-fiber and a higher intensity γ-fiber was observed in the final texture. In agreement with previous reports, a higher intensity γ-fiber (as compared with other components in this work) can be observed in the ODF map of 770-10 and 800-10 samples, however, the α-fiber is totally absent which can be attributed to the formation of austenite nuclei in high intercritical temperatures. As a result, the samples with a higher volume fraction of austenite (higher intercritical annealing temperature) resist the rotation of ferrite grains towards their ideal orientations more severely and therefore, the intensity of rolling fibers in the final texture will decline. Overall, all three DP samples reveal extremely weak texture with the maximum intensities of 1.53, 1.37, and 1.32 × R for 770-10, 800-10, and 830-10 samples, respectively. The γ-fiber intensity diminishes by increasing the intercritical temperature progressively. This is due to the high stored strain energy (SSE) related to the components located on the γ-fiber with a high Taylor factor. In other words, it can be stated that the γ-fiber is extremely unstable when the recrystallization is taking place, and each component located on this fiber can be a probable site for the nucleation of recrystallized grains with random non-rolling orientations [ 23 , 49 ]. To be more precise, γ-fiber reveals 1.42 and 1.19 × R in the 770-10 and 800-10 samples; and by further increasing the intercritical annealing temperature to 830 °C, the γ-fiber completely disappears ( Fig. 12 (a–c)). The γ-fiber in the 770-10 sample is concentrated around {111}<112> and {111}<110> components with 1.34 and 1.30 × R intensities, respectively. The 770-10 sample ODF map in φ 2  = 0° also exhibits a <012>//ND fiber with a moderate intensity of 1.19 × R ( Fig. 12 (a)). Moving on to the 800-10 sample in  Fig. 12 (b), the overall texture intensity was reduced by more intense recrystallization and growth in elevated temperatures. The ODF map for φ 2  = 0° exhibits higher intensities close to Cube ({001}<100>) and Rotated Cube ({011}<100>) components on θ-fiber (<001>//ND) with 1.19 and 1.13 × R, respectively. In addition, a weak {011}<011> component with 1.1 × R was developed and the <012>//ND fiber was totally eliminated. Also, for φ 2  = 45°, the presence of partial ε-fiber (<011>//TD) can be noticed including the Rotated Cube, {112}<111>, and {111}<112> components with 1.13, 1.25, and 1.37 × R intensities, in order. With the examination of  Fig. 12 (c), for the 830-10 sample both the γ-fiber and partial ε-fiber are eliminated, giving rise to <023>//ND in φ 2  = 0° section and <122>//ND in φ 2  = 45° section with the mean intensities of 1.21 and 1.07 × R, respectively. Moreover, both Cube and Rotated Cube components were removed but the intensity of {011}<011> component was maintained. Therefore, increasing the temperature of the intercritical annealing in the process of producing dual-phase steels significantly reduces the intensity of γ-fiber and the overall intensity of the texture.

The Vickers hardness results presented in  Fig. 13 
                      , exhibit much higher hardness values in DP samples compared to the initial sample. This is mainly ascribed to the replacement of pearlite with martensite in DP samples. The martensite transformation is accompanied by volumetric expansion leading to the formation of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) in ferrite and in the vicinity of ferrite-martensite interfaces. This will significantly increase the hardness of ferrite and the corresponding DP sample. Naturally, the increment of V m  leads to a higher density of GNDs and higher hardening of the ferrite phase [ 11 , 16 , 23 , 41 , 46 ]. Furthermore, the supersaturated martensite phase exhibits higher hardness than pearlite colonies and enhances the hardness values in the DP samples. Moreover, the transfer of dislocations from a ferrite grain to a martensite island is difficult due to the different crystallographic structures of the two phases. This combined with high dislocation density in the martensite will contribute to increasing hardness values in DP samples [ 11 ]. As expected, by the increment in V m,  the hardness values are increased which is in accordance with previous works [ 2 , 24 , 37 , 40 , 55 , 66 ]. However,  Fig. 13  shows that the increase in hardness with increasing intercritical annealing temperature is not sharp. This result can be related to the decrease in martensite hardness (as a result of reducing the martensite carbon content) with increasing annealing temperature. In general, with increasing the intercritical annealing temperature, the martensite fraction increases and the martensite hardness decreases. The effects of increasing martensite fraction and decreasing martensite hardness on the hardness of dual-phase steel are opposite. Therefore, the hardness of the DP steel is determined by the competition between these two factors. According to  Fig. 13 , since the hardness of the DP steel increased with increasing temperature, it can be concluded that the effect of increasing martensite fraction is dominated by the effect of decreasing martensite hardness. However, due to the decrease in martensite hardness, the increase in steel hardness is not significant.

Fig. 14 
                       presents the engineering stress-strain curves for the initial and DP samples along three different directions to RD, from which the detailed report of mechanical properties is extracted and plotted in  Fig. 15 
                      (a–d). The initial sample with the lowest yield and tensile strengths and the highest ductility reveals the yield point phenomenon (YPP) characterized by the existence of transition strain between the elastic and plastic regions related to the presence of the Cottrell atmosphere [ 2 , 24 , 30 ]. All DP samples exhibit higher strength, lower ductility, and the absence of YPP compared to the initial sample. The elimination of the YPP is attributed to the formation of residual stresses and inherently mobile GNDs formed to maintain lattice continuity as a result of austenite to martensite transformation accompanied by volumetric expansion during the quenching of the intercritically annealed samples [ 1 , 11 , 16 , 20 , 21 , 23 , 55 ]. According to  Fig. 14 , except for the 770-10 sample along 45°, all other DP samples demonstrate comparable strength-ductility trade-off indicating that the increment of intercritical annealing temperature and V m  did not necessarily result in the enhancement of strength and the reduction of ductility as opposed to the previous reports [ 25 , 35 , 36 , 46 , 66 , 67 ].

By the examination of the YS and UTS in  Fig. 15 (a and b), it is obvious that the substitution of pearlite with martensite and increasing the strength of ferrite in DP samples has resulted in the enhancement of strength values. As reported in previous work [ 68 ], both the YS and UTS enhance due to reducing the grain size of ferrite. This is owing to the grain boundary strengthening mechanism. Also, Calcagnotto et al. [ 69 ] have stated that decreasing the ferrite grain size reduces the differences in tensile characteristics between martensite and ferrite, resulting in postponing the plastic instability due to increased interface cohesion. As indicated by  Fig. 10 , the difference between V m  by increasing the intercritical annealing temperature is insignificant in the 770-10 and 800-10 samples. Therefore, it is expected that these two samples reveal comparable strength values, which is in agreement with the obtained results. On the other hand, the 830-10 sample exhibits nearly 35 % higher V m  than the 800-10 sample (see  Fig. 10 ). Hence, the improvement of YS for the 830-10 sample is reasonable ( Fig. 15 (a)). However, the UTS values of the 800-10 and 830-10 samples are in the same region, which according to  Fig. 10 , might have originated from the lower d f  in the 800-10 sample, which can be beneficial for increasing the UTS ( Fig. 15 (b)) [ 16 , 44 ]. Moreover, the difference between YS along different tensile test directions is negligible for all DP samples, and no observable trend can be found. The average YS values for the DP samples in the order of increasing the intercritical annealing temperature are 438.3 MPa, 454.6 MPa, and 477.2 MPa, respectively. According to the UTS values along different directions, the only sample that shows intense isotropic behavior is the 830-10 sample due to the weakening of the texture. However, both the 770-10 and 800-10 samples demonstrate higher UTS values along RD compared with TD. The inverse pole figures (IPFs) for the 770-10 and 800-10 samples along the RD and TD axis are depicted in  Fig. 16 
                      . Accordingly, the 770-10 sample along TD reveals a higher concentration around the soft <100> orientation with the elastic modulus of 126 GPa [ 48 ] (much less than the elastic modulus of <110> (214 GPa) and <111> (276 GPa) [ 70 ]). The presence of soft orientation (<100>) parallel to the transverse direction reduces the strength. Therefore, the lower strength along 90° (TD) for the aforementioned sample could be justified. The formation of a band-like microstructure on the RD-ND section along the rolling direction (see  Fig. 4 (a)) can be another reason for the difference in the strength of the 770-10 DP steel in different tensile directions. This band-like microstructure is not observed in the TD-ND section of this sample. Some researchers [ 71–75 ] found the higher strengthening of the banded microstructure from the view of strain-hardening behavior, regarding the band-like microstructure as short fiber reinforcement in composite material. They reported that the dual-phase steels with band-like microstructure exhibit higher strain-hardening and better tensile properties due to the distribution of the strain and the efficiency of the transition of the stress [ 61 , 74 , 75 ]. The IPF maps of the 800-10 sample along RD and TD are nearly identical and the slight difference of YS and UTS values along 0° and 90° can be a direct result of that. However, the noticeable difference in ductility values for the 800-10 sample along the 0° and 90° should be ascribed to the dissimilar dispersion of martensite islands in different sections of the sheet. The average ductility values for the 770-10, 800-10, and 830-10 samples are 19.97 %, 20.43 %, and 19.27 %, respectively ( Fig. 15 (c)). As the V m  for the 770-10 and 800-10 samples are nearly similar, the reduction of d f  from 10.2 μm to 7.2 μm by increasing the annealing temperature can be the pivotal factor in enhancing the strength-ductility balance in the 800-10 sample. However, the 830-10 sample reveals a nearly 30 % higher martensite fraction compared with the 800-10 sample, which has resulted in the lower elongation capacity for the 830-10 sample. Again, the texture weakening for the 830-10 sample has led to a much lower difference in ductility values along different directions. The average energy absorption amounts are 126.8, 137.5, and 130.4 J cm −3  by order of increasing the intercritical annealing temperature ( Fig. 15 (d)). It was reported by several authors [ 29 , 35 , 39 , 42 , 43 ] that the reduction of d f  can significantly enhance the strength-ductility combination. Accordingly, the 800-10 sample with the lowest d f  of 7.2 μm exhibited the best energy absorption values. In addition, the more uniform distribution of martensite islands in the 800-10 and 830-10 samples has resulted in higher energy absorption [ 14 , 24 , 36 ].

Khorasani et al. [ 76 ] produced a DP steel containing 58 % martensite with isolated morphology by applying intercritical annealing to plain low-carbon steel with a composition similar to that of the present study. The yield strength, tensile strength, and ductility of the DP steel with isolated martensite were 377 MPa, 648 MPa, and 36 %, respectively. In the present study, however, the best DP steel had 32 % martensite with chain-like morphology. Despite the much lower martensite content, the yield strength and tensile strength of this DP steel reached 482 MPa and 715 MPa, respectively. However, it's ductility decreased to 21 %. This significant difference in the mechanical properties of the two DP steels is mainly related to the martensite morphology. A comparison of these two studies shows that the formation of martensite with chain-like morphology leads to higher YS and UTS than isolated morphology. In chain-like morphology, martensites have much smaller dimensions compared to isolated martensites. This greatly increases the surface area to volume ratio of martensite in the chain-like morphology and provides more obstacles for dislocation movement during tensile testing. As a result, the strength increases more in the presence of chain-like martensite compared to isolated martensite.

Regarding the initial sample, in our previous work [ 49 ] based on the same initial low-carbon steel sheet, a strong Goss component with 2.9 × R intensity, and two fibers of ζ and γ with intensities of 2.3 and 1.7 × R were observed. Therefore, the corresponding texture is not concentrated heavily in the rolling fibers, which is the reason for the moderate anisotropy of the initial low-carbon sheet. Although the γ-fiber intensity is lessened for the 770-10 and 800-10 samples to be 1.42 and 1.19 × R, the anisotropic behavior of the corresponding samples is intensified. To infer that, it should be noted that the dominance of γ-fiber in the aforementioned samples is intensified as compared to the initial sample, meaning that other non-rolling components are non-existent in the texture. Therefore, the γ-fiber dictates high anisotropy of the mechanical properties in the mentioned samples. Conversely, the 830-10 sample with the absence of γ-fiber demonstrates more isotropic behavior as both %IPA and DEV values have dwindled substantially to 1.6 % and 3.9 MPa, respectively. Moreover, the more homogenous dispersion of martensite islands in the 830-10 sample along with the overall texture weakening as a result of more severe recrystallization and growth in elevated temperatures has resulted in the enhancement of mechanical isotropy. Therefore, the uniform distribution of martensite and reduced overall intensity of texture in dual-phase steels can drastically reduce mechanical anisotropy. The ideal in-plane anisotropy should be around zero, however, the lowest in-plane anisotropy found in this research is 1.6 % for the 830-10 DP steel. Achieving low anisotropy in dual-phase steels is important because of the generation of various multiaxial stress states during the formation of automotive parts and car crashes.

Fig. 18 
                      (a–d), depicts the adjustment of the strain-hardening rate as a function of true strain for the initial and DP samples along different tensile test directions. The initial sample shows a transition stage between the first and the third strain-hardening stages which is ascribed to the YPP while all the other DP samples reveal a typical three-stage strain-hardening behavior. It was reported that [ 2 , 3 , 20 , 37 , 38 , 55 ], the first stage with the highest declining rate (the most strain-hardening capacity) is ascribed to the plastic deformation of the ferrite phase and the glide of GNDs. The second stage with a reduced drop rate is connected to the plastic deformation of the constrained ferrite phase surrounded by martensite islands. The last stage with the least reduction rate (the lowest strain-hardening capacity) is related to the co-deformation of both the ferrite and martensite phases ( Fig. 18 (a)). Furthermore, all DP samples exhibit higher strain-hardening rates compared with the initial sample owing to the replacement of cementite with martensite and the generation of GNDs as a result of martensitic transformation which will work harden the ferrite phase and reduce the back stresses generated by the difference in the mechanical properties of the two phases [ 11 , 36 , 39 , 61 , 66 ]. Regarding the 770-10 sample in  Fig. 18 (b), similar to the trends observed in  Fig. 15 , the strain-hardening rate along 0° is the highest mainly due to the weak <001> orientation along RD which is severely disadvantageous to the mechanical properties. The strain-hardening rate along 0° stretched to 0.144 of true strain while along 90° with a more concentrated <001> orientation, the initial strain-hardening rate was lower and stretched to 0.124 of true strain indicating inferior ductility along the TD axis. With regard to the 800-10 sample in  Fig. 18 (c), the highest initial strain-hardening rate was related to the 800-10 (45°) sample which exhibited the highest YS and UTS compared to other directions ( Fig. 15 (a and b)). However, it could only stretch to 0.12 of true strain, and therefore, both the ductility and energy absorption ( Fig. 15 (c) and (d)) were inferior along 45°. On the contrary, the 800-10 (0°) sample a with a lower initial strain-hardening rate exhibited a lower YS and UTS compared with 45° ( Fig. 15 (a) and (b)) but a higher true strain of 0.144, which resulted in the higher ductility and toughness for this sample ( Fig. 15 (c) and (d)). The 830-10 sample with the weakest overall texture indicated a nearly identical strain-hardening behavior along different directions ( Fig. 18 (d)). In other words, the initial strain-hardening rate was the same which was reflected in the mechanical properties, which exhibited extremely close YS and UTS along different testing directions ( Fig. 15 (a) and (b)). The only slight difference was seen in the strain-hardening curve of the 830-10 (90°) sample with a roughly higher true strain of 0.128, hence achieving better ductility and toughness as indicated in  Fig. 15 (c) and (d). The 830-10 sample also enters the third stage of strain-hardening with a true strain of 0.032, which is essentially lower than the 770-10 and 800-10 samples, which exhibit a true strain of 0.04 at the onset of the third stage. This is attributed to the reduction of martensite carbon content with the increase of V m  according to  Fig. 10  which enhances the martensite plasticity that leads to a higher ability of martensite islands to co-deform with the ferrite matrix [ 2 , 24 , 38 , 66 ].

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs:
In this research, the effect of intercritical annealing temperature on the microstructure, texture, and mechanical anisotropic of DP steel was studied. The important conclusions are: 
                         
                            1. 
                            By the increment of intercritical annealing temperature, the fraction of martensite increased in the manner that the martensite islands became completely interconnected in the 830-10 sample. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            The utilization of ASR was beneficial for achieving a more uniform distribution of martensite islands through thickness which can be observed in RD-ND and TD-ND planes of DP samples. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            The overall texture intensity deteriorated and the γ-fiber disappeared by increasing the intercritical annealing temperature. 
                         
                         
                            4. 
                            The Vickers hardness of DP samples constantly improved owing to the increment of V m  at a gentle rate which was ascribed to the reduction of C m . 
                         
                         
                            5. 
                            All DP samples revealed a continuous yielding behavior and a low-yield ratio. The tensile properties for the 800-10 and 830-10 samples were comparable and superior to the 770-10 sample. 
                         
                         
                            6. 
                            The lowest anisotropy of YS and UTS was observed for the 830-10 sample due to the elimination of γ-fiber and texture weakening.
